scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The origin of Kolkali can be traced back to ancient days when Kalarippayattu, the traditional martial art of Kerala, was in active vogue.
The art form heavily incorporates training methods from Kalarippayattu, including body massage, postures, choreography, and footwork.
Over generations, it evolved into a popular folk and martial tradition performed by both Hindus and Muslims in the Malabar region and Lakshadweep.
on_screen: Map: India · South Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Kolkali is performed on festive and social occasions, such as marriage ceremonies in Lakshadweep.
In Kerala, it is a prominent competitive event in youth festivals like the Kerala School Kalolsavam.
It reflects a shared cultural heritage performed by Hindus and Muslims alike.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performers move in a circular formation, wielding two-foot-long sticks to strike against one another in simulated patterns of attack and defense.
The circle dynamically expands and contracts as the dance progresses.
Dancers execute deep bends, body extensions, leaps, and turns, accompanied by singing and rhythmic footwork.
Watch for Stick Striking Circle.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The percussion music for Kolkali is provided by small cymbals and a smaller kind of Chenda drum.
In Lakshadweep, the leader plays a pair of cymbals, and drum music may be supplemented by an Urumi or a long flute.
Listen for the small cymbals, smaller kind of Chenda drum, Urumi, long flute.

The music features driving percussion from a small Chenda drum and small cymbals, accompanied by group singing. The sound begins at a slow, measured pace and progressively increases in pitch and tempo, driving the dancers toward an energetic climax.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: In Lakshadweep, dancers wear a simple costume consisting of a lungi, a banian, and a scarf over the head.
The performance takes place during community occasions such as marriage ceremonies.
In Kerala, performers participate in cultural festivals, including the Kerala School Kalolsavam.

scenes.title: The people
narration: There are two primary styles of Kolkali in Kerala: the actual Kolkali (which includes Thacholikali and Rajasooyam) and Thekkan Koladi.
Kolkali belongs to a lineage of Kerala performing arts that evolved from Kalarippayattu, alongside related forms such as Parichhamuttumkali, Velakali, Oachirakah, and Yatrakali.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Kolkali is influence of Kalarippayattu: Kolkali borrowed much from Kalarippayattu in its basic body training, postures, and footwork.
Kolkali is sibling of Parichhamuttumkali: A similar shield-and-stick dance sharing roots in Kalarippayattu.
Kolkali is sibling of Velakali: Another traditional Kerala dance evolved from Kalarippayattu.
